What is the difference between TCP and UDP?

TCP and UDP are both transport-layer protocols, but they make very different tradeoffs. TCP is connection-oriented and reliable: it performs a three-way handshake, numbers bytes so they can be reassembled in order, retransmits lost segments, and uses flow and congestion control to adapt to network conditions. UDP is connectionless and unreliable by design: it just sends datagrams with a minimal header and no guarantees about delivery, ordering, or duplication. The practical consequence is that TCP is appropriate when correctness matters more than latency, like web browsing, email, or file transfer, while UDP shines where speed and low overhead beat perfect delivery, like DNS queries, online games, voice, and video streaming. Modern protocols like QUIC layer reliability on top of UDP to get the best of both worlds.
When would QUIC be preferable over both TCP and UDP?

QUIC is preferable whenever you want the reliability of TCP combined with the agility of UDP and modern cryptographic features. Because it runs over UDP, it can be deployed and iterated from user space instead of waiting for kernel upgrades, and it integrates TLS 1.3 directly into its handshake to reduce setup round trips. It also multiplexes independent streams without the head-of-line blocking that TCP imposes on multiplexed protocols like HTTP/2, and it migrates gracefully across network changes because connections are identified by an ID rather than a four-tuple. Browsers and mobile apps benefit most, which is why HTTP/3 and many real-time services have moved to QUIC.

Can you walk me through what happens when I type a URL into my browser?

When you hit enter, the browser first resolves the hostname to an IP address using DNS, checking its own cache, the OS resolver, and finally a recursive DNS server that walks the hierarchy from root to TLD to authoritative nameserver. Once it has an IP, the browser opens a TCP connection to the server on port 80 or 443 and, for HTTPS, performs a TLS handshake to agree on encryption keys and verify the server certificate. It then sends an HTTP request with the method, path, headers, and any body. The server responds with a status code and body, often HTML, which the browser parses, triggering further requests for CSS, JavaScript, and images. Throughout, the browser applies caching, cookies, and security policies, and finally renders the page by building the DOM, CSSOM, and layout tree.
What role does the OSI model play in that picture?

The OSI model is a conceptual framework with seven layers, and each step you saw maps onto one or more of them. DNS resolution and HTTP live at the application layer, TLS sits near the presentation and session layers, TCP operates at the transport layer, IP routing happens at the network layer, and Ethernet or Wi-Fi framing is the data-link layer, with the physical medium underneath. In practice, the internet uses a simpler TCP/IP four-layer model, but OSI remains useful for teaching because it cleanly separates concerns and helps you locate where a given problem lives when you are debugging.

What is DNS and why is it important?

DNS, the Domain Name System, is a distributed hierarchical database that maps human-friendly names like example.com to machine-friendly IP addresses and other records. Without it, you would need to memorize numerical addresses for every service you use. Resolution typically starts at a recursive resolver, which queries a root server, a top-level-domain server, and an authoritative nameserver to find the answer, then caches the result for a time specified by the record's TTL. DNS supports many record types beyond A and AAAA, including MX for mail, CNAME for aliases, TXT for metadata, and NS for delegation. Because the system is so foundational, outages or misconfigurations in DNS often look like the entire internet is broken, even when only the name lookup is failing.
What happens when a DNS record's TTL expires?

When the TTL expires on a cached DNS record, the resolver considers it stale and must query an authoritative source again the next time the name is looked up. Until then, subsequent queries for the same name get the cached answer. Short TTLs make changes propagate quickly but put more load on authoritative servers and slow every cache miss, while long TTLs cache aggressively but delay the visible effect of record changes, which matters when doing DNS-based failover or migrations. Operators often lower TTLs temporarily ahead of a planned change, then raise them once the new records are stable.

What does HTTPS actually protect against?

HTTPS protects against three main threats: eavesdropping, tampering, and impersonation. Because traffic is encrypted with symmetric keys negotiated during the TLS handshake, a passive attacker on the network sees only ciphertext rather than the URLs, form data, or cookies flowing by. The handshake also produces message authentication codes, so any in-flight modification by a man-in-the-middle is detected and the connection is aborted. Finally, the server proves its identity with a certificate signed by a trusted certificate authority, which prevents someone from impersonating the real site. HTTPS does not hide the fact that you contacted a particular server or the rough size and timing of your traffic, and it does nothing about compromised endpoints, so it is one layer of defense rather than a complete security solution.
What does HTTPS not protect against?

HTTPS does not hide metadata like the server you are contacting, the approximate size and timing of your traffic, or the fact that a connection happened at all. It also cannot protect against a compromised endpoint: malware on your machine, a malicious browser extension, or an attacker who has broken into the server can read or modify data before or after the encrypted channel does its work. It does nothing about phishing sites that have valid certificates for lookalike domains, and it assumes the certificate authority ecosystem is trustworthy, which has occasionally failed. Treat HTTPS as a strong but narrow guarantee about the channel, not a blanket safety promise.

What is the purpose of a subnet mask?

A subnet mask tells a host which portion of an IP address identifies the network and which identifies the host within that network. With an IPv4 address and its mask, a machine can compute the network address by a bitwise AND and decide whether a destination is on the same local link or must be reached through a router. For example, a mask of 255.255.255.0 reserves the first 24 bits for the network, leaving 8 bits for up to 254 usable host addresses. Modern notation expresses the same idea more compactly using CIDR, like /24. Subnetting lets administrators carve large address blocks into smaller segments that match organizational structure and broadcast domains.

How does NAT work and why do we use it?

Network Address Translation lets many devices on a private network share a single public IP address. When an internal host opens a connection outward, the NAT gateway rewrites the source address and port to its own public address and a chosen port, and it records that mapping in a translation table. Return traffic arriving at the public address and port is matched against the table and rewritten back to the original private destination. The primary motivation has been IPv4 address exhaustion, because public addresses are scarce while RFC1918 private ranges are plentiful. A side effect is that inbound connections to internal hosts do not work without explicit port forwarding, which provides a crude form of firewalling. IPv6 makes NAT largely unnecessary but it remains dominant on IPv4.
Why is NAT less needed in IPv6?

IPv6 has such a vast address space that every device can have its own globally unique address, so the original driver for NAT, sharing scarce public IPv4 addresses, simply does not apply. Networks can assign public routable addresses to internal hosts and use stateful firewalling to control inbound traffic, preserving security without rewriting addresses. That lets protocols that struggle with NAT, like certain peer-to-peer and real-time applications, work more naturally. A few deployments still use IPv6 network prefix translation for operational reasons, but the default assumption flips: hosts get globally reachable addresses, and policy decides which can be contacted.

What is a three-way handshake in TCP?

The three-way handshake is how two hosts agree to open a TCP connection and synchronize initial sequence numbers. The client sends a SYN segment carrying its chosen starting sequence number. The server replies with a SYN-ACK that acknowledges the client's sequence and proposes its own starting sequence. The client then sends an ACK confirming the server's sequence, at which point both sides have verified the other can send and receive and they can begin exchanging data. This exchange defends against stale duplicates from prior connections and provides a small amount of protection against blind spoofing, because an attacker who cannot see the traffic must guess the server's initial sequence number correctly to inject packets.

What is the difference between a switch and a router?

A switch operates primarily at the data-link layer and forwards Ethernet frames within a single local network by learning which MAC addresses sit on which ports. It builds a forwarding table by observing traffic and delivers frames only to the relevant port rather than broadcasting everywhere, which dramatically improves efficiency. A router operates at the network layer and forwards IP packets between different networks based on a routing table that maps destination prefixes to next hops. Routers also handle tasks switches do not, like NAT, firewalling, and participating in routing protocols. A simple way to remember it is that switches connect devices within a network, while routers connect networks to each other.

What does a load balancer do?

A load balancer distributes incoming client requests across a pool of backend servers so that no single instance is overwhelmed and so that failures of individual backends are transparent to clients. Layer 4 load balancers operate on TCP or UDP connections and forward based on addresses and ports, while layer 7 load balancers understand HTTP and can make routing decisions based on paths, hostnames, headers, or cookies. Common distribution strategies include round robin, least connections, and consistent hashing, with health checks removing unhealthy backends from rotation. Beyond scaling and availability, load balancers often terminate TLS, add caching, enforce rate limits, and provide observability across all traffic entering a service.
What is the difference between layer 4 and layer 7 load balancing?

A layer 4 load balancer works at the transport layer, distributing TCP or UDP connections based on IP addresses and ports without looking inside the payload. This makes it fast and protocol-agnostic but unable to make intelligent choices based on content. A layer 7 load balancer understands application protocols like HTTP, so it can route based on hostnames, paths, headers, cookies, or other request details. That enables features like content-based routing, TLS termination, header rewriting, and advanced authentication. Layer 7 is more flexible and richer but introduces per-request processing cost and more operational complexity than plain layer 4.

What is the purpose of a firewall?

A firewall is a policy enforcement point that decides which network traffic is allowed to cross a boundary based on rules. Stateless packet-filtering firewalls inspect each packet in isolation against rules about source, destination, port, and protocol. Stateful firewalls track connection state so they can allow return traffic for connections the internal network initiated while blocking unsolicited inbound attempts. Next-generation firewalls add deep packet inspection, application awareness, and threat intelligence feeds. Firewalls are most useful as one layer in defense in depth: they reduce exposure and contain lateral movement, but they cannot protect against attacks that travel over allowed channels or originate from inside the boundary.

What is the role of a CDN?

A content delivery network is a globally distributed set of caching servers that sit close to end users and serve content on behalf of origin servers. When a user requests a static asset like an image, script, or video segment, the CDN's DNS or anycast routing sends them to a nearby edge server, which returns a cached copy if it has one or fetches from the origin and stores it for future requests. The result is lower latency, reduced origin load, and better resilience against traffic spikes or regional outages. Modern CDNs also deliver dynamic content through optimized network paths, terminate TLS at the edge, mitigate DDoS attacks, and execute small compute workloads near users for personalization.
What is the role of an edge versus origin server in a CDN?

The edge is the set of caching servers spread around the world that actually serve users, while the origin is the source of truth behind them. When an edge server lacks a cached copy of a requested object, it fetches from the origin and stores the result for future hits, applying caching rules from the origin's headers. The origin holds authoritative data, runs application logic, and deals with writes, while edges handle the huge volume of reads close to users. Well-designed CDNs try to keep origins lightly loaded even during traffic spikes, turning them into something closer to a deployment target than a request handler.

How does a VPN work at a high level?

A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel between your device and a VPN server, making it appear as if your traffic originates from that server rather than your real network. The client and server authenticate each other and negotiate keys, then wrap each outgoing IP packet inside another encrypted packet addressed to the VPN endpoint. The endpoint decrypts the inner packet and forwards it to the internet or to a private corporate network, with return traffic flowing back the same way. This shields your traffic from observers on the local network and hides your origin IP from remote services, though the VPN provider itself sees the underlying traffic and must be trusted. Enterprise VPNs mainly exist to safely extend access to internal resources over untrusted networks.

What is the difference between IPv4 and IPv6?

IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses and supports roughly four billion unique hosts, which has proven insufficient as the internet grew. IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, providing a practically inexhaustible address space and making widespread NAT unnecessary. Beyond size, IPv6 simplifies the header, eliminates broadcasts in favor of multicast and anycast, builds in autoconfiguration through SLAAC, and has better support for mandatory IPsec. Notation also differs: IPv4 uses dotted decimal like 192.0.2.1, while IPv6 uses colon-separated hex groups with allowed zero compression. Adoption has been gradual because of inertia and the effectiveness of NAT, so for years to come networks will run dual-stack with both protocols active side by side.

What is the HTTP status code 301 versus 302?

Both codes are redirects, but they carry different semantics. 301 means moved permanently: clients and search engines are expected to update their stored references to the new URL, and compliant caches may store the redirect for a long time. 302 means found, originally described as moved temporarily: clients should follow the redirect for this request but keep using the original URL for future ones. In practice, 302 has a muddled history around whether the method may change from POST to GET during the redirect, which is why 303 and 307 exist to make the behavior explicit. Picking the right code matters for SEO, browser caching, and API clients that make decisions based on the response.
So when should you prefer 303 or 307?

Use 303 See Other when the response indicates that the client should fetch a different resource with a GET, regardless of the original request method. This is the right choice after a successful POST that should redirect the user to a confirmation page and is the classic post-redirect-get pattern. Use 307 Temporary Redirect when you want to preserve the original request method and body in the redirected request, so a POST stays a POST. The 308 Permanent Redirect behaves like 301 but also preserves method and body. These explicit codes avoid the ambiguity that accumulated around the historical behavior of 302.

What is a socket in network programming?

A socket is an endpoint for sending and receiving data across a network, exposed to programs as a file-like handle. Creating a socket involves choosing an address family like IPv4 or IPv6, a type like stream for TCP or datagram for UDP, and optionally a specific protocol. A server binds a socket to a local address and port, listens for connections, and accepts them one by one, while a client connects to a remote address and port. Once connected, both sides read and write bytes through the socket, with the operating system kernel handling segmentation, reliability, and routing underneath. Sockets are the dominant abstraction that most higher-level networking libraries and frameworks ultimately sit on top of.

Why is port 443 associated with HTTPS?

Port 443 is the well-known TCP port assigned by IANA for HTTP over TLS, just as port 80 is assigned for plain HTTP. Well-known ports exist so clients know where to reach common services without configuration: when you type an HTTPS URL, your browser implicitly connects to port 443 on the target host unless the URL specifies otherwise. The assignment itself is administrative convention rather than a technical requirement, and you can run an HTTPS service on any port if clients are willing to specify it. Using the standard port matters because firewalls, corporate proxies, and client defaults expect it, and non-standard ports often get blocked or break tooling.
Can a non-standard port still be secure?

Yes, the cryptographic properties of TLS do not depend on port 443 at all; TLS on any port provides the same confidentiality, integrity, and authentication guarantees. The downsides of non-standard ports are practical rather than cryptographic. Some corporate networks only allow TLS on standard ports, breaking client access. Clients and scanners may assume non-standard ports host non-standard services, producing false alarms or misbehaving tools. Running on a non-standard port is sometimes useful for internal services or to avoid conflicts on a host, but it is not a substitute for proper authentication, correct TLS configuration, sensible certificate management, and access controls. Treat the port choice as an operational detail and the real security as coming from the cryptography and policy layers above it.

What is TLS and how does the handshake establish trust?

Transport Layer Security is the cryptographic protocol that secures most of the internet's application traffic, and it sits between TCP and application protocols like HTTP. During the handshake, the client and server agree on a cipher suite, exchange random values, and perform a key exchange using algorithms like ECDHE to derive shared symmetric session keys without ever sending them over the wire. The server presents a certificate signed by a trusted certificate authority, and the client validates the signature chain, the hostname, and the expiry. If validation succeeds, both sides derive keys and switch to encrypted, authenticated records for the rest of the session. TLS 1.3 streamlines the handshake significantly and removes legacy algorithms that had accumulated weaknesses.

What is ARP used for?

The Address Resolution Protocol maps an IP address on a local network to the corresponding MAC address needed to actually deliver an Ethernet frame. When a host wants to send a packet to an IP on its subnet, it first checks its ARP cache for a known mapping. If there is no entry, it broadcasts an ARP request asking who has that IP, and the owner replies with its MAC address. The requester caches the answer for a while so subsequent packets avoid the broadcast. ARP only works within a single broadcast domain, and it is inherently trust-based, which is why ARP spoofing attacks are possible on networks without additional protections like DHCP snooping or dynamic ARP inspection.
Why can ARP spoofing work on a local network?

ARP was designed for cooperative local networks and has no built-in authentication; any host can emit an ARP reply claiming ownership of any IP, and receivers generally accept it and update their caches. An attacker on the same subnet can therefore convince victims that the attacker's MAC owns the gateway's IP, routing traffic through their machine for inspection or tampering. Mitigations live mostly in the switch: features like dynamic ARP inspection validate replies against a trusted binding table populated by DHCP snooping, and secure architectures increasingly rely on encrypted protocols like HTTPS and SSH so that even a successful ARP spoofer cannot decrypt what they see.

What is bandwidth versus latency?

Bandwidth is the rate at which data can be transferred, typically measured in bits per second, and it tells you how much can flow in a given period. Latency is the time it takes for a single piece of data to travel from source to destination, typically measured in milliseconds, and it is dominated by distance and the number of hops. The analogy is a highway: bandwidth is how many lanes are open, and latency is how long a single car takes to complete the trip. A fat link with long latency can still make chatty protocols feel slow because each small exchange waits a full round trip, which is why techniques like pipelining, multiplexing, and edge caching matter alongside raw bandwidth upgrades.

How does BGP work on the internet?

The Border Gateway Protocol is the routing protocol that glues autonomous systems together on the internet. Each AS, typically an ISP or large network operator, advertises the IP prefixes it can deliver to its BGP neighbors, along with path attributes describing the route. Neighbors propagate these announcements with their own AS added to the path, and each router runs a path-selection algorithm that prefers routes based on policy, path length, and other attributes. Because BGP is policy driven rather than purely shortest-path, operators can express business relationships like customer, peer, and provider. The protocol's trust model is famously loose, which is why incidents like route leaks and hijacks can redirect substantial traffic until operators respond.

What is the difference between stateful and stateless protocols?

A stateful protocol remembers information about the client across multiple exchanges, while a stateless protocol treats each request in isolation with no memory of prior ones. FTP is a classic stateful protocol: it tracks the current directory, authentication, and transfer mode over the life of the control connection. HTTP, by contrast, is nominally stateless: the server does not inherently remember that two requests came from the same client. State in HTTP applications is built on top using cookies, tokens, or server-side session stores. Statelessness makes horizontal scaling and caching easier because any server can handle any request, but it pushes complexity into the application when continuity is needed.
What are the main limitations of WebSocket?

WebSocket gives you a raw duplex channel, but that is both its strength and its weakness. It does not handle reconnection automatically, so applications must detect drops and resume sensibly, often with exponential backoff and state reconciliation. It lacks built-in message acknowledgement beyond TCP, so exactly-once delivery and ordering across reconnects must be designed in. Proxies, load balancers, and CDNs need explicit support to route long-lived connections correctly, and scaling requires sticky routing or a pub-sub layer because each server only sees its connected clients. For simple cases like occasional updates, server-sent events or long polling can be simpler choices.

What is WebSocket and when would you use it?

WebSocket is a protocol that upgrades an HTTP connection into a persistent, full-duplex channel over a single TCP socket. The handshake starts as a normal HTTP request with an Upgrade header, and once the server accepts, the connection switches to a framed binary or text protocol where either side can push messages without waiting to be asked. This is a good fit for real-time applications like chat, collaborative editors, live dashboards, and multiplayer games, where polling would be wasteful and latency-sensitive. For workloads that fit a request-response pattern, plain HTTP or server-sent events are usually simpler. WebSocket does not provide built-in reconnection, backpressure, or ordering guarantees beyond TCP, so applications typically layer their own conventions on top.

What is a proxy server?

A proxy is an intermediary that accepts requests from clients and forwards them to other servers on their behalf, often applying transformations or policies in the middle. A forward proxy sits in front of clients and is typically used for caching, content filtering, or anonymity. A reverse proxy sits in front of servers and is used for load balancing, TLS termination, request routing, and shielding backends from the internet. Transparent proxies intercept traffic without client awareness, usually enforced at the network layer. Proxies can inspect and modify protocol headers and bodies, which makes them powerful, but for encrypted traffic like HTTPS they either terminate TLS with their own certificate or merely tunnel opaque bytes.
What protections did DNS over TLS and HTTPS add?

DNS over TLS and DNS over HTTPS move DNS queries from plaintext UDP or TCP to encrypted, authenticated connections to a resolver of the client's choosing. This hides the names a user is looking up from observers on the network, prevents on-path tampering with answers, and lets clients validate they are really talking to the resolver they meant to contact. The tradeoff is a shift of visibility and trust toward that resolver, since it now sees every query. DoH in particular is controversial in operational settings because it can bypass network-level filtering and monitoring that some environments rely on, so deployments vary by context.

Why does DNS use UDP and sometimes TCP?

DNS traditionally uses UDP on port 53 because queries and answers are usually small and latency sensitive, and the overhead of establishing a TCP connection for every lookup would be excessive. UDP fits cleanly: one packet out, one packet back, no handshake, no state to tear down. DNS falls back to TCP when responses exceed the size that reliably fits in a single UDP datagram, typically 512 bytes in classic DNS or up to 4096 with EDNS(0). Zone transfers between authoritative servers always use TCP because they are large and require reliable delivery. Newer variants like DNS over TLS and DNS over HTTPS use TCP-based transports specifically to gain privacy and integrity that plain UDP cannot provide.

What is a man-in-the-middle attack?

A man-in-the-middle attack is one where an adversary positions themselves between two parties so that all traffic flows through them, allowing the attacker to read, modify, or inject messages while each endpoint believes it is talking directly to the other. On a local network this is often achieved through ARP spoofing, rogue Wi-Fi access points, or DHCP hijacking, and upstream it can come from BGP attacks or compromised routers. Defenses focus on authenticating the peer and the channel: TLS certificate validation, SSH host key checking, and protocols like IPsec or QUIC that bind keys to identities. Users can also reduce risk by preferring encrypted protocols, verifying certificates, and avoiding untrusted networks for sensitive activities.
What does the SameSite cookie attribute do?

SameSite controls when browsers attach a cookie to cross-site requests. Strict blocks the cookie on any cross-site request, which is safest but can break legitimate navigations from other origins. Lax allows cookies on top-level navigations like clicking a link but blocks them on cross-site requests that would be dangerous, like POST submissions and embedded resource loads; this is a sensible default for session cookies. None requires Secure and attaches the cookie on cross-site requests, which is needed for legitimate third-party use cases. SameSite is a significant defense against CSRF and tracking, and modern browsers default unspecified cookies to Lax.

What is the purpose of HTTP cookies?

Cookies are small pieces of data the server asks the browser to store and send back with subsequent requests to the same origin, giving an otherwise stateless protocol a way to recognize a returning client. They are widely used for session identifiers after login, user preferences, and tracking. Cookies carry attributes that control their scope and lifetime, including domain, path, expiration, Secure to require HTTPS, HttpOnly to hide them from JavaScript, and SameSite to mitigate cross-site request forgery. Modern privacy concerns have tightened browser defaults around third-party cookies, and many tracking uses are migrating to first-party storage or server-side techniques. Cookies remain central to how login sessions work on the web.

What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric networking topologies?

In a symmetric topology, nodes have roughly equivalent roles and capabilities, so any peer can talk to any other peer with similar responsibilities, as in a classic peer-to-peer network. In an asymmetric topology, there is a clear distinction between clients and servers or between core and edge, with different nodes playing different structural roles. Most of the internet today is asymmetric in practice: end users contact a relatively small number of high-capacity servers or CDNs, rather than exchanging data directly with each other. Symmetric architectures can be more resilient and avoid single points of failure but require more coordination, while asymmetric architectures concentrate complexity and capacity where it can be managed and scaled cost-effectively.

What is the difference between simplex, half-duplex, and full-duplex?

These terms describe who can transmit when. Simplex means communication is one way only: one side transmits and the other only receives, as with broadcast radio. Half-duplex means both sides can transmit but not simultaneously, so they must take turns, as with classic walkie-talkies or old shared-medium Ethernet using hubs. Full-duplex means both sides can transmit and receive at the same time over separate channels, as with modern switched Ethernet using twisted-pair cabling and separate transmit and receive wires. Full-duplex typically doubles effective throughput compared with half-duplex on the same link and eliminates collisions, which is why modern wired networks overwhelmingly run full-duplex.
Why does QUIC use connection IDs instead of the IP-port four-tuple?

Connection IDs let a QUIC session survive changes in the underlying network path. If a mobile device switches from Wi-Fi to cellular, its IP address changes and a traditional TCP connection would break, forcing reestablishment and often losing in-flight work. With QUIC, the endpoints identify each other by an opaque connection ID carried in the packets, so the new path is recognized as the same session once a short validation confirms ownership. This is a big quality-of-life win for mobile users and long-lived sessions, and it also provides some defense against linkability because connection IDs can rotate without tearing down the underlying session.

What is QUIC and why was it designed?

QUIC is a transport protocol that runs over UDP and provides the reliability, ordering, and congestion control of TCP along with integrated TLS 1.3 encryption. It was designed to solve several problems that became painful on modern web traffic: slow connection setup from separate TCP and TLS handshakes, head-of-line blocking when one lost packet stalls all multiplexed streams, and poor handling of client mobility between networks. QUIC combines the handshake into one or two round trips, multiplexes independent streams that do not block each other, and uses connection identifiers so sessions survive IP changes. It forms the transport layer for HTTP/3 and is widely deployed by major platforms.

What is the difference between unicast, multicast, and broadcast?

Unicast is one-to-one: a packet has a single destination address and is delivered only to that host. Broadcast is one-to-all within a given scope, usually a local subnet: any host on the network receives the packet, which is useful for discovery protocols but can be wasteful at scale. Multicast is one-to-many: a packet is addressed to a group, and only hosts that have joined that group receive it, with routers and switches cooperating to replicate it efficiently along the delivery tree. Multicast is well suited to streaming video to many subscribers on a managed network, while the public internet predominantly uses unicast with overlay or application-layer replication.

What is the difference between a process and a thread?

A process is an independent execution context with its own virtual address space, file descriptors, and accounting, while a thread is a unit of execution within a process that shares the address space with its sibling threads. Creating a process is relatively expensive because the operating system must set up new memory mappings and other resources, while creating a thread is cheaper since most state is inherited. Threads in the same process can communicate through shared memory with careful synchronization, whereas processes typically communicate through explicit IPC like pipes, sockets, or shared memory segments. Threads within a process share a fate: a crash in one can take the entire process down, which is an argument for process-level isolation when fault tolerance is critical.

What is virtual memory?

Virtual memory is an abstraction that gives each process its own apparent linear address space while the operating system maps those virtual addresses to physical memory or to disk as needed. The translation happens through page tables managed by the kernel and walked in hardware by the MMU, with a TLB caching recent translations for speed. Virtual memory enables isolation between processes, since no process can address another's memory directly, and it enables overcommit through paging to disk when physical RAM is exhausted. It also supports useful tricks like memory-mapped files, copy-on-write after fork, and shared libraries mapped once and used by many processes. The cost is the complexity and occasional performance cliffs when pages must be fetched from disk.
What is a page fault?

A page fault is the exception raised when a process touches a virtual page whose mapping is not currently valid. Minor faults happen when the page is in memory but not wired into the process's page table, for example after a copy-on-write split or when the kernel lazily populates a just-allocated region. Major faults happen when the page must be read from disk, such as paging in from swap or loading from a memory-mapped file. The kernel's fault handler decides how to satisfy the request, updates the page tables, and resumes the instruction. Excessive major faults manifest as thrashing, where the system spends more time paging than computing.

What is a context switch?

A context switch is the act of saving the execution state of one thread or process and restoring that of another so the CPU can run it instead. The saved state includes registers, the program counter, stack pointer, and memory-management state like the page-table base, and for processes it also invalidates or tags TLB entries so addresses do not bleed across. Context switches happen on preemption, when a task blocks on I/O, or on explicit yields. What is CPU cache and why does it matter?

CPU cache is small, fast memory embedded near or inside the processor that holds recently used data and instructions so the CPU can access them far faster than going out to main memory. Typical designs have multiple levels: L1 is tiny and fastest, L2 is larger and a bit slower, and L3 is shared across cores. Caches exploit temporal and spatial locality, assuming that code touches the same data repeatedly and tends to access nearby addresses in sequence. Because DRAM latency is hundreds of cycles while L1 hits are a few, cache behavior often dominates performance more than raw instruction count, which is why data layout and access patterns matter so much for tight loops.
What practical lessons follow from cache effects?

Programs that respect cache locality run much faster than those that do not, even when they have identical algorithmic complexity. Practical lessons include preferring arrays over linked lists for traversal, laying out structs so fields used together sit near each other, iterating multidimensional arrays in the order they are stored in memory, and batching work to reuse recently loaded data. Tight loops that fit in L1 can be orders of magnitude faster than those that constantly spill to memory. Profilers and performance counters help identify cache-bound hotspots, and data structure choices are often the single biggest lever available to improve performance on modern CPUs.

What is pipelining in CPU design?

Pipelining overlaps the execution of multiple instructions by dividing their processing into stages, like fetch, decode, execute, memory, and writeback, so that while one instruction is in the execute stage another is being decoded and a third is being fetched. Under ideal conditions this multiplies throughput compared with a non-pipelined design that finishes one instruction before starting the next. Hazards complicate the picture: data hazards when one instruction needs the result of a recent one, control hazards at branches, and structural hazards when units are busy. Modern processors use forwarding, branch prediction, out-of-order execution, and speculation to keep the pipeline fed, which is why real-world CPUs can retire several instructions per cycle.

What is instruction-level parallelism?

Instruction-level parallelism is the ability of a processor to execute multiple instructions at the same time, overlapping work from nearby parts of the program. Techniques include pipelining, superscalar issue where multiple instructions start per cycle across several functional units, and out-of-order execution where the processor dispatches ready instructions without waiting for older ones stuck on a slow dependency. Branch prediction and speculation let the CPU keep going past conditional branches without stalling. Compilers help by scheduling instructions to expose independence and avoiding false dependencies. The ceiling on ILP in ordinary code is finite, which is a major reason multi-core and vector parallelism became important for further scaling.
What limits instruction-level parallelism in real code?

Real code is full of dependencies: the result of one instruction feeds the next, forming chains that cannot be parallelized no matter how many execution units are available. Branches break straight-line execution, and even with good prediction, misses cost cycles. Memory accesses introduce unpredictable latency because a cache miss stalls anything that depends on the value. Finally, the instruction set and the CPU's width put hard upper bounds on how much parallelism any single thread can extract. Beyond those limits, further speedups come from coarser-grained parallelism like threads, SIMD vectorization, and specialized accelerators, each with its own programming model.

What is cache coherence?

Cache coherence is the set of rules that keep multiple caches in a shared-memory system in agreement about the current value of each cacheable location. Without coherence, two cores could each have their own copy of the same address and happily read stale data. Protocols like MESI and its variants track for each cache line whether it is modified, exclusive, shared, or invalid, and use bus transactions or directory messages to enforce a consistent view: when one core writes, others with copies are invalidated or updated. Coherence has significant hardware cost, particularly for heavily contended lines, which is why false sharing and lock ping-ponging can be so damaging to multi-threaded performance.

What is the memory hierarchy?

The memory hierarchy is the layered arrangement of storage in a computer, from fastest and smallest near the CPU to largest and slowest at the far end. It typically runs from CPU registers, to L1, L2, and L3 caches, to main memory, to solid-state storage, to spinning disks, to network and archival storage. Each level is an order of magnitude or more slower but larger than the one above it, and software performance depends heavily on how well its access patterns fit this hierarchy. Operating systems and hardware work together through prefetching, caching, and paging to keep hot data as close to the CPU as possible while still offering the illusion of a flat address space.
How does false sharing hurt performance?

False sharing happens when two threads repeatedly modify different variables that happen to sit on the same cache line. The coherence protocol treats the line as contested and bounces it between the cores' caches, even though the threads are logically independent. The result can be orders of magnitude worse than the same code with the variables on separate lines. Mitigations include padding hot per-thread variables to the cache-line size, using thread-local storage, and laying out data structures so concurrently modified fields end up on different lines. Performance counters that track coherence traffic make false sharing visible, which is otherwise easy to miss.

What is out-of-order execution?

Out-of-order execution lets a CPU reorder instructions at runtime to keep its execution units busy, as long as the program's observable behavior remains that of the original order. The processor fetches and decodes instructions in program order, then dispatches them to a reservation station or scheduler that tracks which have all their inputs ready. Ready instructions execute in parallel across multiple functional units, and a reorder buffer retires results in program order so state updates and exceptions appear sequential. Out-of-order designs hide latency from cache misses and long operations but pay for that with far more complex hardware, and speculative side effects have famously enabled transient-execution vulnerabilities like Spectre.

What is SIMD?

CPUs expose this through instruction sets like SSE, AVX, and NEON, with special wide registers and matching arithmetic instructions. Compilers can auto-vectorize simple loops, but squeezing full performance often requires intrinsics or libraries. GPUs push SIMD much further with thousands of lanes executing in lockstep, which is why they dominate large neural-network workloads.

What is Von Neumann architecture?

The Von Neumann architecture is a design where a single memory stores both instructions and data, and a single bus connects memory to the CPU, which repeatedly fetches an instruction, decodes it, and executes it. It was a major simplification over earlier computers that had separate program and data stores, and nearly all general-purpose computers today follow this model at a high level. The main downside is the Von Neumann bottleneck: every instruction and every data access competes for the same memory path, which is why modern systems soften the model with caches, separate L1 instruction and data caches, and sophisticated memory hierarchies even though the logical picture remains Von Neumann.

What is Harvard architecture?

Harvard architecture separates instruction memory from data memory, each with its own bus, so the CPU can fetch an instruction and read or write data simultaneously. It is most common in digital signal processors, microcontrollers, and embedded systems where deterministic timing and throughput matter and where programs live in read-only flash while data sits in RAM. The choice shapes tradeoffs in flexibility, as mixing code and data, like in JIT compilation or self-modifying code, requires explicit synchronization on Harvard-like designs.

What is a GPU versus a CPU?

A CPU is optimized for low-latency execution of a small number of threads with complex control flow, featuring large caches, aggressive branch prediction, and out-of-order execution. A GPU is optimized for throughput on many parallel threads performing similar work, with thousands of simpler cores, wide SIMD execution, and massive memory bandwidth, at the cost of higher latency per individual operation and limited support for irregular control flow. Graphics pipelines, matrix-heavy deep learning, physics simulations, and large-scale scientific computing fit GPUs well. General-purpose code with heavy branching and serial dependencies fits CPUs better. Modern systems deliberately combine both, offloading throughput-bound kernels to the GPU while the CPU handles the rest.
What is a TPU and how does it compare to a GPU?

A tensor processing unit is an accelerator designed specifically for the dense linear algebra that dominates deep-learning workloads, particularly matrix multiplications and convolutions. Compared with a general-purpose GPU, a TPU trades flexibility for specialization: it often uses lower-precision arithmetic, a systolic-array matrix engine, and tight integration with a host runtime like TensorFlow or JAX. The result is very high throughput per watt on its target workloads, but less suitability for tasks outside that narrow mold, such as graphics or irregular compute. Cloud providers offer TPUs alongside GPUs, and choice between them often comes down to software-stack compatibility and cost-per-result on the specific model.

What does it mean for a processor to be superscalar?

What is endianness?

Endianness describes the order in which multi-byte values are stored in memory. In big-endian, the most significant byte comes first at the lowest address, matching how humans write numbers left to right. In little-endian, the least significant byte comes first, which simplifies some arithmetic hardware and is the convention for x86 and many ARM configurations. Endianness usually only matters when serializing, sharing memory with other systems, or interpreting raw bytes, because within a consistent system the details are hidden.

What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning?

What is overfitting in machine learning?

Overfitting is when a model learns the training data so specifically, including its noise and idiosyncrasies, that it performs much worse on new data. It shows up as a widening gap between training performance, which looks great, and validation or test performance, which does not improve or gets worse. Causes include a model with too much capacity relative to the amount of data, too little regularization, or leakage of test information during development. Remedies include gathering more or more diverse data, stopping training earlier, adding regularization like weight decay or dropout, simplifying the model, and using cross-validation to get an honest estimate of generalization before committing to decisions.

What is gradient descent intuitively?

Gradient descent is an optimization algorithm that searches for parameters minimizing a loss function by repeatedly stepping downhill along the steepest descent direction. At each step, you compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the parameters, which points uphill, then update the parameters by subtracting a small multiple of that gradient. The multiplier is the learning rate, and choosing it is part of the art: too small and training crawls, too large and it overshoots or diverges. Stochastic and mini-batch variants use samples of data at each step, trading some noise for much faster progress, and modern optimizers like Adam add momentum and per-parameter adaptive scaling on top of this core idea.

What is a neural network in plain terms?

A neural network is a parameterized function made by composing many simple units, often called neurons, each computing a weighted sum of its inputs passed through a non-linear function. Layers of such units process the input in stages, with later layers operating on representations produced by earlier ones. Training adjusts the weights so the network's output matches desired outputs on training data, typically through gradient descent driven by the loss's gradient propagated backward through the network. With enough data and compute, networks of this form can learn very rich mappings for tasks like image recognition, language modeling, and speech recognition, which is why they have become the dominant tool in modern machine learning.
How is overfitting related to model capacity?

Model capacity is roughly how many distinct functions a model can represent. Very low-capacity models cannot even fit the training data well and show high bias. As capacity grows, training loss falls and generalization improves up to a point, beyond which the model begins to fit peculiarities of the training set that do not reflect the underlying distribution, hurting test performance. Classic methods like decision trees, polynomial regression, and neural networks all show this U-shaped generalization curve to some extent. Modern over-parameterized deep networks reveal a more complicated picture, where generalization can improve again at very high capacity, but smaller models still benefit from matching capacity to data.

What is backpropagation?

Backpropagation is the algorithm for efficiently computing gradients of a neural network's loss with respect to all its parameters. It applies the chain rule systematically in reverse through the computation graph: starting from the loss, it works backward layer by layer, multiplying local Jacobians to accumulate partial derivatives. The cost is roughly the same as a forward pass, which is what makes training deep networks feasible at scale. Modern deep-learning frameworks automate this through reverse-mode automatic differentiation, so practitioners write forward computations and get gradients for free. Despite decades of refinement around it, backpropagation remains the workhorse of almost all neural-network training today.

What is the bias-variance tradeoff?

The bias-variance tradeoff describes two sources of error in a learned model. Bias is error from a model too simple to capture the true relationship, leading to systematic underfitting. Variance is error from a model so sensitive to its training data that small changes produce very different predictions, leading to overfitting. Increasing model complexity tends to reduce bias and raise variance, while regularization and simpler models do the opposite. The goal is to find a point that balances them for the given amount of data and noise. Modern over-parameterized deep networks complicate the classical picture, producing double-descent phenomena where very large models can regain generalization, but the intuition still helps guide decisions about capacity and regularization.

What is the difference between classification and regression?

Classification predicts a discrete label from a finite set, like spam versus not spam, or which of a thousand ImageNet categories an image belongs to. Regression predicts a continuous value, like a temperature forecast, a house price, or a click-through rate. The two tasks differ in loss functions used to train models, in evaluation metrics, and often in the shape of the final layer of a neural network: a classifier typically produces probabilities via softmax or sigmoid, while a regressor produces raw real values. Many problems sit on the boundary: ordinal regression, for example, predicts ordered categories, and some regression tasks are discretized into classification buckets for practical reasons.
What is the intuition behind momentum in optimization?

Momentum adds a fraction of the previous update to the current one, so the optimizer accumulates a velocity along directions where gradients consistently point the same way and dampens oscillation in directions where they flip. The effect is similar to a ball rolling down a surface: it speeds up along gentle slopes, keeps going briefly through flat regions, and is less distracted by narrow ridges. In high-dimensional non-convex landscapes, this dramatically speeds up training and helps the optimizer escape shallow local minima. Modern variants like Adam combine momentum with per-parameter adaptive learning rates, inheriting momentum's smoothing while also handling scale differences between parameters.

What is a loss function?

A loss function is a measurable notion of how wrong a model's predictions are on a batch of data, and minimizing it is the explicit goal of training. Despite its name, logistic regression is a classifier, not a regressor. Both models share simple, interpretable structure and efficient training, and both generalize: linear regression extends to multivariate targets, while logistic regression extends to multiple classes through softmax. What is a training set versus a test set?

What is the difference between authentication and authorization?

Authentication is proving who you are, while authorization is deciding what you are allowed to do. What is SQL injection?

What is cross-site scripting?

What is cross-site request forgery?

Nothing the attacker puts in a parameter can turn into a new clause, change the meaning of an existing one, or terminate the statement. What is the principle of least privilege?

The principle of least privilege says that every user, process, and service should have exactly the permissions it needs to do its job and no more. Applied broadly, it shrinks the blast radius when credentials are stolen, bugs are exploited, or humans make mistakes. What is a zero-day vulnerability?

A zero-day vulnerability is a security flaw that is being exploited or publicly disclosed before the vendor has had a chance to release a patch, meaning defenders have zero days of advance notice to prepare. Because no fix exists, affected systems must rely on mitigations like disabling features, applying work-arounds, tightening network controls, or isolating critical assets until a patch is available. Responsible disclosure programs try to prevent zero-days by giving vendors a coordinated window to fix issues before details go public, while bug bounty programs reward researchers for reporting rather than selling to malicious buyers.

What is phishing?

Phishing is a social-engineering attack that tricks people into revealing credentials, personal information, or authorizing actions, typically through messages that impersonate trusted senders. What is defense in depth?

Defense in depth is the strategy of layering multiple independent security controls so that the failure of any one does not lead to catastrophic compromise. A single system might rely on network segmentation, host hardening, application-level input validation, strong authentication, authorization checks, audit logging, and detection tooling, each designed to catch different classes of attack. The attacker must defeat every layer in sequence, while a defender gets many chances to observe or stop them. Defense in depth acknowledges that no control is perfect and that threats evolve, so resilience comes from diversity and redundancy of protections rather than any one silver bullet.

What is ransomware?

Ransomware is malware that encrypts a victim's data, or increasingly also exfiltrates it, and demands payment for decryption keys and silence. Modern operations often work as criminal enterprises with affiliate programs, leak sites for extortion, and negotiation channels. Entry vectors include phishing, exposed remote desktop services, vulnerable perimeter devices, and compromised suppliers. Defenses combine prevention, like patching and multi-factor authentication, with preparedness, like tested offline backups, segmentation that limits lateral movement, endpoint detection and response, and incident-response plans. Paying a ransom is legally and practically fraught: it can fund further attacks and does not guarantee recovery, but organizations sometimes have no better option.
What are some concrete ways to enforce least privilege?

Concrete enforcement mechanisms include role-based access control with well-defined roles scoped to specific resources, just-in-time access elevation that grants temporary privileges with audit trails, short-lived credentials issued from a central authority instead of long-lived keys in configuration files, and per-service database accounts with rights limited to the tables each service actually uses. At the infrastructure layer, cloud IAM policies should be written as narrowly as possible and reviewed with tools that flag overly broad permissions. Process controls like regular access reviews, offboarding automation, and separation of duties complement the technical controls, because stale permissions accumulate if no one is responsible for removing them.

What is a buffer overflow?

A buffer overflow is a bug where a program writes more data to a memory buffer than it has space for, spilling into adjacent memory. In languages without memory safety, this can corrupt nearby variables or, classically, overwrite a function return address on the stack with attacker-controlled data, redirecting execution to injected code. Buffer overflows have historically been one of the most devastating classes of vulnerabilities. Mitigations include stack canaries that detect overwrites, non-executable stacks, address space layout randomization, compiler fortification, and moving to memory-safe languages like Rust and Go. Defensive coding practices, bounds-checked libraries, and aggressive use of sanitizers during testing also help.

What is a honeypot?

A honeypot is a system or service set up specifically to attract attackers, not to provide real value, so that defenders can detect reconnaissance, capture techniques, and study threats in a controlled environment. Low-interaction honeypots emulate services at a shallow level and are easy to deploy but can be fingerprinted. High-interaction honeypots run real services and give attackers more rope, yielding richer information at the cost of operational complexity and risk of abuse. At scale, networks of honeypots called honeynets feed research on malware, botnets, and emerging campaigns. Inside enterprises, canary tokens and decoy systems raise alarms the moment attackers interact with something nobody legitimate should touch.
How do defenders usually learn about a zero-day?

Defenders typically learn about a zero-day in one of several ways: through incident investigation when suspicious behavior leads to discovering a previously unknown exploit, through threat-intelligence sharing between vendors, governments, and private firms, through researcher disclosures that arrive alongside or shortly before public discussion, or through the vendor's own telemetry and bug-bounty submissions. Once aware, the vendor races to develop a patch while defenders deploy mitigations and detection rules. Because that window between discovery and widespread patching is when attacks are most effective, speed in each step matters, which is why coordinated disclosure programs and rapid-patching infrastructure have become central to modern security operations.

What is the difference between a virus, a worm, and a trojan?

A virus is malicious code that attaches to a legitimate program or file and propagates when that host is run or opened. A worm is self-propagating malware that spreads through networks without needing a host program, typically by exploiting vulnerabilities on reachable services. A trojan is software that pretends to be benign while hiding a malicious payload, relying on users to install or execute it voluntarily. Modern threats often blend categories, like a trojan dropper that deploys ransomware and worming capabilities. The categories mainly describe propagation strategy rather than purpose; the damage, whether data theft, destruction, or remote control, can be similar across them.

What is a security token or JWT?

A security token is a piece of data that represents a claim about an authenticated user or service and can be presented to an API to get access. JSON Web Tokens are a popular format where a JSON payload with claims is encoded and signed or encrypted so that recipients can verify its authenticity without a shared-session database. Claims often include the subject, issuer, audience, expiration, and custom permissions. JWTs are convenient because they are stateless and easy to pass through HTTP, but they come with pitfalls: choosing the right signing algorithm, rotating keys, keeping lifetimes short, and avoiding pitfalls like accepting tokens with the none algorithm or failing to validate audiences.

What is an SQL injection mitigation beyond prepared statements?

Prepared statements remain the primary defense, but layered mitigations matter in depth. Input validation rejects obviously malformed values early, not as a replacement for parameterization. Least-privilege database accounts restrict what any compromised query can do, for instance denying data-definition rights to application connections. Web application firewalls can catch known injection patterns before they reach the application. ORMs typically parameterize by default and discourage raw concatenation, but raw query support still needs the same discipline. Code review, static analysis, and dynamic testing tools hunt for risky string concatenation patterns. Finally, limiting error messages in production prevents attackers from using verbose database errors to shape their payloads.

What is symmetric session encryption versus end-to-end encryption?

In symmetric session encryption like ordinary HTTPS, traffic is encrypted between a client and the server it talks to, but the server itself sees plaintext once it decrypts. Intermediaries along the way only see ciphertext, which is enough for most confidentiality needs against network adversaries. In end-to-end encryption, messages are encrypted on the sender's device and decrypted only on the recipient's device, so even the service provider sees nothing but ciphertext. This is the right model when users do not want to trust the operator of the service, as in modern messaging apps, but it makes server-side search, content scanning, and multi-device synchronization much harder to implement.

What is security through obscurity?

Security through obscurity is the strategy of relying on secrecy about how a system works to protect it, such as hiding URLs, not publishing algorithms, or obfuscating code. It is generally considered weak on its own because determined attackers eventually uncover implementation details through reverse engineering, leaks, or shared sources, and once the details are out the system has no real protection left. Modern practice follows Kerckhoffs's principle: a well-designed system should remain secure even if everything about its construction is public, with confidentiality resting on secret keys rather than secret designs. Obscurity can add modest friction as part of defense in depth, but never as the primary protection.
What is content security policy?

A content security policy is a set of rules, delivered through an HTTP header, that tells the browser which sources it is allowed to load scripts, styles, images, frames, and other resources from. Well-configured CSP acts as a strong defense against cross-site scripting: even if an attacker injects a script tag, the browser refuses to execute it unless the source is whitelisted or the script carries a valid nonce or hash. CSP also constrains dangerous practices like inline scripts and eval, pushing developers toward safer patterns. Deploying it well is nontrivial because it can break existing third-party integrations, but when done correctly it dramatically reduces the impact of many web vulnerabilities.

What is secure coding?

Secure coding is the practice of writing software in ways that resist common attacks and fail safely when something goes wrong. It includes input validation, output encoding for the right context, parameterized database queries, safe memory handling in languages that allow unsafe memory access, careful use of cryptographic libraries rather than home-grown algorithms, secrets management, avoiding logging sensitive data, and robust error handling. Beyond individual practices, secure coding is supported by processes: threat modeling, code review with a security lens, static and dynamic analysis in CI, dependency scanning, and a culture that treats security as a first-class concern rather than a last-minute audit.
